title: The Real Wolf of Wall Street Scam

beats.say: The film made it look like one long party. Yachts, money, chaos. But behind the real Wolf of Wall Street was a scheme that cost ordinary investors around two hundred million dollars.
That's the figure from Jordan Belfort's own plea agreement. Losses of around two hundred million dollars, taken from investors who trusted his brokers.

vis.label: investor losses, per the plea agreement

beats.say: So how did it actually work? Let's break down the real scheme, step by step, and why the same playbook is still used today.
Part one. Stratton Oakmont.
Jordan Belfort ran a brokerage firm on Long Island called Stratton Oakmont. At one point it employed more than a thousand stockbrokers.
It was what's called a boiler room. A packed office of young salespeople, cold calling people all day with scripted pitches and enormous pressure to close.

The brokers followed carefully written scripts. Build rapport. Create excitement. Overcome every objection. And never let the customer off the phone without a sale. Many of the brokers were young, with little financial training, but they were taught to sound like experts.

vis.title: The sales script
items: Never hang up without a sale

beats.say: The brokers weren't selling the stocks of big famous companies. They were mainly selling penny stocks. Tiny, little known companies, with shares that cost very little and were rarely traded.
Part two. The pump.
Here's the scheme. It's called a pump and dump. First, insiders quietly get hold of lots of shares in a small company, often very cheaply.
Then come the phone calls. Thousands of them. Brokers tell investors about an amazing small company that's about to take off. Buy now, before everyone else does.

vis.text: Buy now, before everyone else does.

beats.say: Often, the brokers would first win a customer's trust by recommending solid, well known stocks that made a little money. Once the customer trusted them, the brokers would push the risky penny stocks.

vis.text: First earn trust. Then push the risky stuff.

beats.say: As investors buy in, demand pushes the price up. The share price rises, which makes the pitch even easier. Look, it's already going up.
Part three. The dump.
Then, at the top, the insiders sell. They dump their cheap shares onto the investors who've just bought in at high prices.
Without fake demand holding it up, the price collapses. The insiders walk away with huge profits. The ordinary investors are left holding shares worth a fraction of what they paid.

Why does this hurt so much? Because penny stocks have very few buyers. When the insiders sell big blocks, there's almost nobody on the other side to buy. The price can fall incredibly fast, and ordinary investors can't get out.

vis.title: Why the crash is so fast

beats.say: And the brokers would often discourage clients from selling, so the insiders could get out first. That's the dark heart of a pump and dump.
Part four. The lifestyle.
The money funded an extraordinary lifestyle. Mansions, cars, wild parties, and a huge yacht called Nadine, which sank off the coast of Sardinia in nineteen ninety six.
Inside the office, the culture was famously wild. But the real engine was simple. Every sale meant commission for the brokers, and every pump meant profits for the people at the top.
Stratton also helped bring real companies to the stock market, including the shoe brand Steve Madden. But regulators had been watching the firm for years.
Part five. The fall.
In nineteen ninety six, Stratton Oakmont was expelled by the industry regulator, the NASD. In nineteen ninety nine, Belfort was indicted for securities fraud and money laundering.
He pleaded guilty and cooperated with the FBI, even wearing a wire against former associates. In exchange, he got a lighter sentence. Four years, of which he served about twenty two months.
He was also ordered to repay more than one hundred and ten million dollars to victims. For years, prosecutors and his lawyers argued about how much he'd actually paid back.
Years later, reports said the restitution obligation had finally been completed. But for many victims, decades had passed since they lost their money.

vis.text: Decades later, the bill was finally paid.

beats.say: Part six. The movie.
In twenty thirteen, Martin Scorsese turned Belfort's memoir into The Wolf of Wall Street, with Leonardo DiCaprio. It was a huge hit. And Belfort became a famous sales speaker.
Critics argued that the film showed the party, but barely showed the victims. Ordinary people who lost savings never got their own movie.

vis.text: The victims never got a movie.

beats.say: And pump and dump schemes haven't gone away. Today, they often happen with small stocks and crypto coins promoted on social media, in group chats and by influencers.

vis.title: Spot a modern pump and dump
items: Hype in chats and social media
Promoters who don't say they own it

beats.say: So when someone you don't know is desperate for you to buy something right now, ask yourself one question. If it's such a great deal, why do they need my money?

vis.text: Why do they need my money?
